title: Electrical Characteristics and the vibration performance of PVDF - Cu MEMS Piezoelectric Vibrational Energy Harvester
venue: 2020 International Conference on Power, Energy, Control and Transmission Systems (ICPECTS)

sections.heading: Electrical Characteristics and the vibration performance of PVDF – Cu MEMS Piezoelectric Vibrational Energy Harvester
sections.text: Cyril Robinson Azariah John Chelliah Department of Nanotechnology, Institute of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Saveetha School of Engineering, Saveetha Institute of Medical and Technical Sciences, Chennai – 602105 cyrilrobinsonazariahj.sse@saveetha.com

sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
For the past few decades, the researchers have keen interest in developing an energy harvester for low power devices. Several MEMS based piezoelectric architectures have been employed. In this work, the electrical energy to be harvested from mechanical vibrations made of polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) piezoelectric material of thickness $1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , $2 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ and $3 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ on $2 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ thick copper $\mathrm { ( C u ) }$ substrate. The structure was simulated under three different predetermined vibrations, using an online numerical simulation tool. By translating the vibration and voltage signals into dimensional variables, an empirical relationship was found in which the output power can be related to the vibration characteristics, the piezoelectric material properties, and the resistive load. The simulated results were recorded and tabulated. This PVDF piezoelectric cantilever-based MEMS energy harvester that operates under ambient excitation of natural frequency band of 191 to $2 4 1 \ \mathrm { \ H z }$ , within a base acceleration of 2.9 to $4 . 7 \mathrm { g }$ produces an average output power of $0 . 1 5 \mathrm { u } - 1 . 6 5 \mathrm { u }$ $[ \mathrm { u W } ]$ and 0.3 volts at 1u farad load capacitance. These results are way promising to power up potential biodevices and low frequency applications.

Keywords: PVDF, Cu, Piezoelectric, MEMS, Nanohub

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
MEMS Piezoelectric Vibration Energy Harvesting (MPVEH) is an online cloud-associated numerical simulation tool designed to simulate the dynamic behaviour of the Piezoelectric Energy Harvesting MEMS.[1] This device is composed of a cantilevered beam of piezoelectric layers which includes both bimorphic and unimorphic) with a proof mass at the end as shown in Figure 1.

These devices use the principle of direct piezoelectric effect to convert the energy of the vibrating surface to electrical current as shown in Figure 2.[2], [3] This is done by shaking a cantilevered beam that is coupled to a piezoelectric film. When the beam resonates, the piezoelectric material accumulates electrical charges and delivers them to the circuit. The first phase of the simulation is designing the beam geometry.

![](images/c6833888c7a2ee1b1ddbba0c69c4238c8bbd53dc2a579a815797cb638e806517.jpg)

The aim of this paper brings light on to simulate the harvested electrical power from mechanical vibrations using a piezoelectric cantilevered beam. Piezoelectric materials have been shown to be effective for vibration utilisation systems of small dimensions. This could enable low-consumption electronic devices to be powered by mechanical oscillations. Physical modelling of piezoelectric cantilevered beams has been addressed in various publications. In this work, this electromechanical model is incorporated into an online numerical simulation tool that helps design and characterise these devices and serves as an educational resource.[6]

sections.heading: METHODOLOGY
sections.text:
A system of ordinary differential equations is derived for modelling the piezoelectric beam's first oscillation mode (corrected lumped-parameter model). These equations are integrated using the 4th order Runge-Kutta algorithm that describes the instantaneous tip displacement and output voltage. The numerical method is implemented in Octave, and the Rappture Toolkit incorporates a GUI. After the dynamic equation has been resolved, the programme conducts a frequency analysis and calculates some relevant harvesting process statistics such as the specific power and resonance frequencies. Other features include simulating a full-wave rectifier circuit, testing the device with sources of measured vibrations, frequency sweeps, and impulse inputs.[7]

![](images/2c373a61d65195cb89fadccdbe0a968d4e230a775c60a76a7392f5b4d13dc7ad.jpg)  
Figure 4 Screenshots of the input of the simulation tool and frequency sweep parameters

First, we choose the thickness of the piezoelectric as $1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , $2 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ and $3 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ and the thickness of the substrate as 200 $\mu \mathrm { m }$ . The length of the device is $1 0 \mathrm { m m }$ , the length of the proof mass is $0 . 1 \mathrm { m m }$ and its width $5 \mathrm { { m m } }$ as shown in Figure 4. The gap is $2 5 \mathrm { m m }$ . In this work, there are 2 number of piezoelectric layers and its connection is series type. In the mechanical properties, the proof mass is considered as $1 ~ \mathrm { m g }$ and end-mass density as $1 9 0 0 0 \mathrm { k g } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ . PVDF is the piezoelectric material and copper substrate were chosen. The frequency sweep, random vibration, hammer hit and predetermined vibrations were enabled. The frequency range were swept from $1 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 0 \mathrm { K H z }$ . The amplitude considered to be $1 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The exponential decay constant is kept at zero. The final stage is the selection of some other required parameters in three groups: environmental conditions, circuit topology, and simulation length. Environmental conditions change surrounding air density and viscosity. This affects measuring aerodynamic drag, which becomes important at very small scales. The circuit topology supports two options: resistive load and full-wave rectifier. In both cases, a load and capacitance must be specified.

In this work, a full-wave rectifier is used to provide a threshold voltage for the diodes since they are best modelled within the design. Finally, simulation duration is suggested. This determines the simulation time as a reference frequency, which in most situations would be the normal beam frequency. Technically, the software takes an internal judgement that often relies on the form of input vibrations: if it is a frequency sweep, it is measured at the lowest frequency; but, if the lowest frequency is too low, it uses the natural frequency as a guide such that the simulation is not too long.[8], [9]

sections.heading: CONCLUSION
sections.text:
![](images/930a487c883ca8b605be873752f2d5a885d6bc23e149d5a8ad35660185fede96.jpg)  
Figure 6 power vs time

To conclude, electrical energy is harvested from mechanical vibrations made of $1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , $2 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $3 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ thick piezoelectric content of polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) on $2 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ thick copper (Cu) substrates and successfully simulated using the MPVEH instrument. The optimum load is about 1uF, and its overall output power is about 1.5-15 pico W, which is very limited for practical use. It is completely a very good guide for MEMS designers to create a more intricate piezoelectric micro-power generator or the various perspectives for improving the power harvested for bio implants or bio compatible devices and for very low frequency applications.
